# Isaiah 47: verse-by-verse research notes

**What the sources say overall:** Most of the commentators read the chapter the same way. It is a taunt-song in which God humbles proud Babylon for three things: cruelty to Judah, arrogance, and trust in magic and astrology. Real disagreements show up in only a few places: who speaks v. 4, whether v. 8 is self-deification, how to translate v. 11, who the "traders" of v. 15 are, and whether "Babylon" also stands for a later corrupt church.

**Structure:** The Pulpit Commentary calls the chapter "A SONG OF TRIUMPH OVER THE FALL OF BABYLON," divided into four strophes: vers. 1-4; 5-7; 8-11; and 12-15. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/47-1.htm

---

**v. 1**
- **Ellicott:** Babylon, personified as till now unconquered, is told to leave her throne and sit in the dust like a menial slave. "Tender" and "delicate" point to the luxury Babylon was known for, which was now to end. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/47-1.htm
- **Barnes:** Sitting on the ground and throwing dust on the head is a common biblical sign of humiliation and mourning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-1.htm
- **What "virgin" means (commentators disagree):**
  - **Calvin (Reformed):** "Virgin" is used not because she was modest or chaste, but because she had been brought up softly and delicately like "virgins," and had never been forced by enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/47-1.html
  - **Pulpit:** Rejects "unconquered," since the "virgin daughter" means the Babylonian people as distinct from the city, and Babylon had been taken by the Assyrians some half-dozen times. It also notes that Babylon was never, after her capture by Cyrus, the capital of a kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
  - **Coffman:** The title reflects not God's estimate of her character, but her position in the world at that time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/47-1.html
- **Wesley (Methodist):** She is called virgin because she was tender and delicate. "No throne" means for her: the empire is taken from her and passed to the Persians. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-47.html

**v. 2**
- **Pulpit:** She must do the hard work commonly allotted to female slaves. On the road into captivity, captives would have to wade through streams and expose themselves in doing so. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Ellicott:** The scene is, of course, to be taken symbolically, not literally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-2.htm
- **Geneva notes (Reformed):** The things in which she takes her greatest pride will be made vile, from head to foot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-2.htm

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** The humiliation God puts on Babylon is exactly what she put on Judah and Jerusalem, and God cannot be talked out of His judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/
- **Pulpit:** It renders the last line literally as "I shall not meet a man," meaning "I shall not find any one to oppose me." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Bob Utley (bible.org):** It may mean that no one could intercede for Babylon, or that no human was powerful enough in prayer to stop YHWH's plan. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20921

**v. 4: who is speaking?**
- **Guzik:** Isaiah seems unable to help himself and praises God and boasts in his redeemer. Through Bultema, Guzik ties the Hebrew *goel* (kinsman-redeemer) to Christ, who paid with His blood on Golgotha to ransom His people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/
- **Ellicott:** Reads the verse as Israel's song of praise over Babylon's overthrow, unless it was originally a marginal note. He finds a parallel in the fall of mystical Babylon in Revelation 18:20. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-4.htm
- **Pulpit (citing Cheyne):** Cheyne suspects it is "the marginal note of a sympathetic scribe". If the verse is kept, Pulpit reads it as the Jewish Church's aside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Another reading (Poole/Gill on the same page):** Some join it to v. 3: "I will take vengeance... saith our Redeemer". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-4.htm

**v. 5**
- **Pulpit:** The fallen people are told to hide their shame in silence and darkness, like disgraced people who shrink from being seen. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-5.htm
- **Barnes:** "Darkness" means a place of mourning; people in deep grief shut out the light from their homes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-5.htm
- **Gill:** It could mean captivity or imprisonment, since prison houses are dark, or the state of the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-5.htm

**v. 6**
- **Guzik:** Babylon conquered Judah only because God was angry with His people and used Babylon as His instrument. Even so, they still should have shown mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/
- **Geneva notes:** Babylon abused God's judgments, thinking He would completely cast Israel off, so instead of pitying their misery it increased it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-6.htm
- **Barnes:** The Scriptures treat honouring the aged as a sacred duty, and contempt for old age as a serious crime. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-6.htm
- **Pulpit, on how badly the exiles were treated:** We know very little about how the Jewish exiles were generally treated. The words may be fulfilled by the "cruelties which disfigured the first days of the Babylonian triumph". Pulpit adds that there is no reason to give this passage an allegorical meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm

**v. 7**
- **Pulpit:** The expectation that things will continue is a basic human instinct. Babylon still should have remembered that all things come to an end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Babylon knew earthly things are uncertain but did not lay this to heart or apply it to herself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_047.cfm
- **Bultema (quoted by Guzik):** Applies vv. 5–11 to the corrupt Church, which he says placed a cross on its steeple instead of on its shoulders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/

**v. 8: is "I am, and there is none besides me" self-deification? (commentators disagree)**
- **Ellicott, yes:** The boast deliberately echoes Jehovah's claims about Himself, and she practically deified herself. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/47-8.htm
- **Pulpit, no:** "This is not self-deification, but only a boast of superiority to all other earthly powers", with a parallel in Zephaniah 2:15. Pulpit also cites Herodotus: the people made light of Cyrus's siege. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Preceptaustin devotional:** It is a claim true of God alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_devotionals_4

**v. 9**
- **Pulpit:** "In one day" points to the day Cyrus took the city in 539 BC. Pulpit lists three kinds of Babylonian magic (spells and talismans, incantations, omens and horoscopes). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Chuck Smith:** Paraphrases the boast as "Our husbands will never be slain in battle", which God overturns in one night. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/47-1.html
- **Utley (bible.org):** For all her magic Babylon could not protect herself, which shows that occult practices are corrupt and useless. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20921

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** The proud trust in their continuing wickedness to cover the tracks of their earlier sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/
- **Ellicott:** Babylon took "Might is Right" as its law and in practice denied a Ruler who sees and judges. The "wisdom" meant here is astrology and magic. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/47-10.htm
- **Pulpit:** "Wickedness" here means incantations and spells, and Babylon's astronomy turned into astrology. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Sinners often think they are safe because they think their wickedness is secret, but their security will be their ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/47.htm

**v. 11: a translation question**
- **Pulpit:** The Vulgate, Vitringa and others read "thou shalt not know from whence it riseth." Most modern commentators read "how to charm it away" (as the BSB does), and the parallel lines favour that reading. "Put it off" literally means to expiate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Wesley:** This fits the history: Babylon was surprised by Cyrus while feeling completely secure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-47.html
- **Guzik:** Links it to Daniel 5 and to the principle that God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/

**v. 12**
- **Pulpit (quoting Cheyne):** The verse has "a strongly ironical tinge, reminding us of Elijah's language to the priests of Baal". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Guzik:** If they had real spiritual power, they should be able to save Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/

**v. 13**
- **Pulpit:** The three titles are scarcely three classes of persons, but the same class under three names. Pulpit separates legitimate star-mapping from astrology and compares the "consultations" of Daniel 2 and 5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/47.htm
- **Grogan (quoted by Guzik):** In Babylonia the intellectual and the magical were intertwined. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/

**v. 14**
- **Ellicott:** The destroying flame is nothing like the fire on the hearth where a man can sit and warm himself. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/47-14.htm
- **Pulpit:** Stubble is a favourite metaphor with Isaiah for extreme weakness. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/47-14.htm

**v. 15: who are the "traders"? (commentators disagree)**
- **Barnes, merchants:** Read literally as merchants, but the point is that destruction would come upon the business, not necessarily on each trader. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-15.htm
- **Wesley, both groups:** By moving the words around, he makes the sorcerers useless and the merchants scatter, every one to his own quarter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-47.html
- **Kretzmann (Lutheran), the magicians themselves:** The astrologers, wizards and magicians did a flourishing business at the citizens' expense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/isaiah-47.html
- **Coffman, either:** The traffickers, whether merchants or traders in the black arts, will not be around when needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/47-15.html
- **Guzik:** Those who will not find salvation in the Lord have no one who can save them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-47/

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ: does "Babylon" also mean a later church or Rome?
- **Henry:** She calls herself virgin though she was the mother of harlots. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/47-1.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** Links v. 1 to the beast's throne in Revelation 13:2, and v. 15 to the merchants of mystical Babylon in Revelation 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/47-1.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-47.html
- **An unnamed commentator on Bible Hub:** One excerpt on the v. 1 page says outright that the church of Rome... is no other than the great whore. The excerpt does not name its author. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/47-1.htm
- **Bultema (via Guzik, Pentecostal/Calvary-style site):** Applies vv. 5–11 to a corrupt church (see v. 7).
- **Pulpit, the opposite view:** Rejects allegorical meanings for at least v. 6.

## What I couldn't find
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I found no comment on this chapter from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Modern scholarship:** I found no NET Bible translator notes or bibleodyssey.org pages. The only modern-critical points are those Pulpit reports from Cheyne (v. 4 as a scribe's note; the irony in v. 12).
- **Lutheran and Anglican:** Apart from Kretzmann (v. 15), I found nothing from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or Anglican sources.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.

I left all of these out rather than guess.
